newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO general says no major Bosnia withdrawal yet.
newsitem.headline: NATO general says no major Bosnia withdrawal yet.

text.p: The NATO-led peace force in Bosnia will not make major withdrawals until delayed municipal elections have take place there, the head of the alliance's military committee said on Wednesday.
General Klaus Naumann told a news conference the peace implementation force -- IFOR -- had to be prepared for trouble in the campaigning leading up to the municipal polls.

"It is too early to give a detailed assessment of what the deferral of the municipal elections will mean for the troop levels, but a preliminary assessment shows that there will not be much room for significant drawdowns before the elections," he said.
Javier Solana, Secretary-General of NATO, said at the news conference that he expected the municipal elections to take place in late November or early December.
IFOR has 55,000 troops in Bosnia. Its one-year mandate expires on December 24 and steady reductions in the force had been expected to begin after the Bosnian national elections last Saturday.
However, Naumann warned that while there had been no major incidents surrounding the national elections he did not expect the same to be true of the municipal polls.
"The national elections strained IFOR forces to the limit and we feel we will need to maintain a similar level of presence up to the municipal elections which will be much more difficult," he said.
"We have to be prepared for unpleasant events. We are prepared for trouble."

Solana said that far from running down now that the national polls had been completed, IFOR would remain very active in policing Bosnia and helping the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) prepare for the municipal elections.
"The utmost vigilance will be required. We expect continued compliance with the Dayton peace agreement and IFOR will enforce it if necessary," he said.
The OSCE announced in August that the municipal polls would be postponed because of voter registration irregularities and other problems.
Solana and Naumann both repeatedly stressed that IFOR would not outstay its mandate -- regardless of whether or not the municipal elections had been held by December 24.
But Solana also said that there was no question of the world simply turning its back on Bosnia after the IFOR withdrawal.
"It is too early to talk about what is going to happen after December 24. But I can tell you now quite clearly that the international community will not abandon Bosnia," he said.
In that context, Solana said NATO's policy-making North Atlantic Council decided at its regular weekly meeting on Wednesday to give the green light to the setting up of a new headquarters in Bosnia.
Ostensibly the new headquarters is to replace the IFOR operational headquarters and oversee the withdrawal.
But there is speculation that it will have a dual role of organising the withdrawal of IFOR and of running whatever replacement force is eventually agreed.

Solana refused to be drawn on the issue. He said the future of Bosnia would be discussed at an informal meeting of NATO defence ministers in the Norwegian city of Bergen on September 24 and 25, although no decision would be taken.
